deep.reconstruction:
The page holds no derivation. It has three kinds of content.

(A) Lecture announcements (German, ink, top; and upside down at the bottom). Riemann will begin his course on the mathematical theory of gravity, magnetism and electricity on Wednesday 2 May in Auditorium V. His public lecture, on special problems from the same areas of physics, will be on Friday 4 May in Auditorium V. The upside-down draft says that this semester he intends to lecture on 'die mathematische Theorie der Schwere, der Electricität und des Magnetismus' on several days a week, 9-10 a.m.
- A Wednesday 2 May with a Friday 4 May fits 1860 (also 1866; Riemann was then ill in Italy).
- My inference: summer semester 1860, the course behind Hattendorff's edition 'Schwere, Elektricität und Magnetismus' (1876). That edition is usually associated with Riemann's summer 1861 lectures, so the year is uncertain.

(B) A heavily corrected Latin problem statement in pencil, in the style of a prize or examination question. The final version reads roughly: 'Determinentur inter superficies tribus lineis rectis datis terminatas eae, quarum radii curvaturae extremi [in]aequales et oppositi sunt [et quae] pari quolibet superficiei [sunt] superficies minima inter omnes iisdem terminis contentas.'
- Translation: among surfaces bounded by three given straight lines, determine those whose principal radii of curvature are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign, and which are, in every part, of least area among all surfaces with the same boundary.
- Modern form: solve the Plateau problem with boundary made of three straight lines. That is, find a surface with mean curvature H = (1/R1 + 1/R2)/2 = 0 (R1 = -R2) that is area-minimising among surfaces with the same boundary.
- A deleted variant says the area of each such piece, or of the total surface, would otherwise be infinite. This reflects that the bounding lines are unbounded, so 'minimal' must be meant locally, piece by piece ('pari quolibet').
- This matches the programme of Riemann's posthumous memoir 'Ueber die Fläche vom kleinsten Inhalt bei gegebener Begrenzung' (Hattendorff, Abh. Göttingen 13, 1867). There he solves Plateau problems for boundaries of straight lines via the Gauss map / Weierstrass-type representation and hypergeometric-type functions.

(C) A second, abandoned Latin problem: 'Duobus cylindris [circularibus] infinitis, quorum axes sunt parallelae, [determinetur ...]', i.e. given two infinite circular cylinders with parallel axes, determine ... The object is cancelled. In the context of the physics course, it is most plausibly the electrostatic or heat potential of two parallel cylinders, solved by bipolar coordinates / conformal mapping. It could also be the minimal surface spanning them; this cannot be decided.

The names 'Herr Hebbe(?), Hofmann(?), Wolf(?), Fischer(?)' (upside down) are probably students or auditors.
errors: The phrase read as 'inaequales et oppositi' must, mathematically, mean principal radii equal in magnitude and opposite in sign (H=0). 'inaequales' is either a misreading of 'aequales' or a slip; only 'aequales et oppositi' characterises minimal surfaces.

The problem as worded is not yet well posed: surfaces bounded by three infinite lines have infinite area, so minimality must be local. Riemann's own deleted clause about infinite area shows he was aware of this.

results.what: Formulation of the Plateau problem for a boundary of three straight lines, with minimal surfaces characterised by principal radii equal and opposite
results.modern_name: Plateau problem for polygonal (straight-line) boundaries; minimal surface H=0
results.usually_credited_to: Characterisation: Meusnier 1776; straight-line Plateau problems: Riemann (posth. 1867), Schwarz (1865 onward), Weierstrass (1866)

results.what: Problem on two infinite parallel circular cylinders (object not stated)
results.modern_name: Probably the two-cylinder potential problem (bipolar coordinates)

results.what: Announcement of the lecture course on gravity, electricity and magnetism

deep.surprise_reason: Riemann's work on minimal surfaces bounded by straight lines is well known from his posthumous 1867 memoir. This page only adds a draft prize/exam-style formulation and a lecture announcement, which give minor dating context.

checkable.asserts: In 1860, 2 May was a Wednesday and 4 May a Friday, consistent with the announcement
The helicoid, a minimal surface containing straight lines, satisfies the minimal surface equation (H=0, i.e. R1=-R2)
Scherk's surface (asymptotic to straight lines) satisfies H=0

transcription_corrections: 'inaequales et oppositi' should probably be 'aequales et oppositi' (or is a slip by Riemann); the mathematics requires equal and opposite radii.
The ink line 'am 2. Mittwoch' is probably just 'am Mittwoch, den 2. Mai'.
The marginal mark '𝔐' at the left of the Latin block is uncertain; it may be a 'W' or a paragraph sign.
